question: Who should I call to talk about hiring a fractional Chief Revenue Officer?
body:
## Direct Answer
Start with the specialized fractional executive firms and RevOps-focused talent networks rather than a generic recruiter — providers like Chief Outsiders, Bench Accounting-style fractional-exec marketplaces, GTM advisory shops, and vetted operator communities are built for this. Your first three calls should be a fractional-exec firm, a peer founder who has hired one, and your own board or lead investor, because each gives you a different lens on fit, price, and urgency. The person you want on the phone is someone who places or has *been* a revenue leader — not a keyword-matching staffing agency.

Hiring a fractional Chief Revenue Officer (fractional CRO) is less like posting a job and more like assembling a short list of trusted intermediaries who understand go-to-market leadership. The reason the "who do I call" question matters so much is that the fractional market is fragmented and largely relationship-driven — there is no single dominant marketplace the way there is for, say, fractional CFOs. Below is a practical map of exactly who to contact, in what order, what to ask them, and how to tell a real revenue operator from a repackaged sales trainer.

## Which types of firms and people actually place fractional CROs?
There are five distinct channels, and most founders only discover two of them before hiring. The first is **specialized fractional-executive firms** — organizations whose entire model is placing part-time C-suite operators into growth-stage companies. These firms typically bench a roster of former VPs of Sales, CROs, and GTM leaders, then match one to your stage, motion, and industry. The advantage is speed and vetting: they have already done reference checks and can put a candidate in front of you within a week. The tradeoff is a premium on top of the operator's rate, and sometimes a bias toward keeping their bench utilized rather than finding your perfect fit.

The second channel is **fractional-talent marketplaces and communities** — platforms and Slack/Circle communities where independent fractional executives list themselves directly. Here you talk to the operator without a firm in the middle, which lowers cost and raises transparency, but shifts the vetting burden onto you. The third is **your own network of founders and operators**, which is statistically where the best fractional hires actually come from: a warm referral from someone who watched the CRO perform is worth more than any résumé. The fourth is **VCs, accelerators, and your board**, who keep informal lists of "operators we'd back again." The fifth, used last, is **generalist executive recruiters and staffing agencies** — useful only if the others run dry, because they rarely understand revenue motion deeply enough to screen well. If you want a deeper framework for matching a leader to your GTM stage, our guide on [scoping revenue leadership](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11133) walks through the stage-to-seniority fit in detail.

![Who should I call to talk about hiring a fractional Chief Revenue Officer — figure 1](/assets/qa/tl9120-b1.jpg)


It helps to understand *why* these five channels exist as separate markets rather than one clearinghouse. Fractional revenue leadership is a young category compared to fractional finance, where a decades-old ecosystem of outsourced-CFO firms already standardized pricing, scope, and expectations. Revenue leadership resisted that standardization for years because the job itself is less portable: a great CRO for a product-led SaaS company selling to developers may be actively wrong for an outbound-heavy company selling six-figure contracts to hospital systems. Motion, buyer, deal size, and sales cycle all change what "good" looks like, so the market never consolidated into a single directory. That fragmentation is exactly why the "who do I call" question is the real question — the search itself is the hard part, and the channel you pick shapes the candidate pool you'll ever see.

A practical consequence is that you should plan to run **two or three channels in parallel**, not sequentially, once you've defined your problem. Founders who work a single channel to exhaustion — say, only their firm's bench — tend to over-index on whoever that channel happens to have available that month. Working a firm, a community, and your own network simultaneously gives you a natural comparison set: three or four candidates from three different sources, evaluated against the same one-paragraph problem statement. That comparison is what protects you from anchoring on the first confident voice, and it costs you almost nothing beyond a few extra intro calls.

![Who should I call to talk about hiring a fractional Chief Revenue Officer — figure 2](/assets/qa/tl9120-b2.jpg)


## Who should I call first, second, and third?
Sequence matters more than most founders realize, because your early calls shape your reference price and your definition of "good." Call your **peer network first** — two or three founders at a similar stage who have hired a fractional CRO in the last 18 months. They will tell you the unvarnished truth about rates, ramp time, and what broke. Call your **board member or lead investor second**, because they have pattern-matched across their portfolio and can often make a single introduction that skips weeks of searching. Only then call the **fractional-exec firms third**, armed with a real budget range and a sharper spec so you can evaluate their bench against a standard instead of being sold one.

The diagram below shows the recommended contact order and what each source is best at surfacing. Notice that the paid firms come *after* your free, high-trust sources — not because firms are bad, but because talking to them first tends to anchor you to their inventory rather than your actual need.

![Who should I call to talk about hiring a fractional Chief Revenue Officer — figure 3](/assets/qa/tl9120-b3.jpg)


```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[You need a fractional CRO] --> B[Call peer founders first]
    B --> C[Call board or lead investor]
    C --> D[Call fractional exec firms]
    D --> E[Call talent marketplaces]
    E --> F[Call generalist recruiters last]
    B --> G[Best for honest rates and ramp truth]
    C --> H[Best for warm vetted intros]
    D --> I[Best for speed and prescreened bench]
```

The logic here is that each source answers a different question. Peers answer "what is this actually like and what should it cost." Investors answer "who is trustworthy and available." Firms answer "who can start next week." When you call them in that order, every later conversation is sharper because you carry forward what the earlier ones taught you. Reverse the order and you risk hiring the first polished pitch you hear.

There is also a timing reason to front-load the free calls. Peer and investor conversations are slow to schedule but fast to pay off — a founder friend might take a few days to get on the phone, but once they do, they hand you a rate range, two names, and a warning in twenty minutes. Firms are the opposite: instant to book, but the meeting is a sales call, and sales calls are optimized to move you toward a decision on the firm's terms and timeline. If you open the process with the slow-to-schedule calls, you use the natural lag productively — while you wait for your peer and your investor to free up, you write your problem statement and clarify your budget. By the time the firm meeting happens, you are a buyer with a spec, not a prospect being qualified. That single shift in posture changes the entire negotiation.

One caveat: sequence is a default, not a religion. If your problem is genuinely urgent — a VP of Sales just quit mid-quarter and the forecast is exposed — you may need to call a firm *first* precisely because speed outranks everything else, and then backfill the peer and investor calls as reference checks on whoever the firm proposes. The point of the ordering is to protect your judgment when you have the luxury of time; when you don't, invert it deliberately and consciously, not by accident.

## What exactly should I say on the first call?
The single biggest mistake is calling before you can describe the problem in revenue terms. Fractional CROs are hired to fix a *specific* failure — a stalled pipeline, a broken handoff between marketing and sales, a founder who can no longer be the top closer, a new motion the team has never run. Before you dial anyone, write one paragraph: what is breaking, what "fixed" looks like in 90 days, and how many hours a week you think you need. This paragraph is your screening tool. A strong fractional operator will react to it with sharp diagnostic questions; a weak one will nod and pitch a generic engagement.

On the call itself, ask four things. First, **"What GTM motions have you personally run and scaled?"** — you want lived experience with *your* motion, whether that is product-led, sales-led, or channel. Second, **"How many companies are you fractional for right now?"** — more than three or four simultaneously usually means diluted attention. Third, **"Walk me through a fractional engagement that didn't work, and why."** — the honest answer reveals more than any success story. Fourth, **"What does your first 30 days look like concretely?"** — a real operator has a repeatable diagnostic-then-build sequence, not vague promises to "align the team." For a structured version of these questions and how to score the answers, see our interview framework on [evaluating fractional revenue leaders](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/aq1158).

Keep the first call short and diagnostic. You are not trying to hire on the phone; you are trying to decide whether this person earns a paid trial project or a deeper working session. The best signal is whether they make *your* problem sharper. If you hang up understanding your own revenue problem better than before, that is a person worth a second conversation — regardless of which channel they came through.

Beyond the four core questions, listen for how the candidate talks about *your team* versus *themselves*. A tell that separates operators from performers is where the credit lands in their stories. Someone who owned real outcomes will naturally describe the reps they hired, the sales manager they promoted, and the systems they left behind that kept working after they left. Someone who was really a solo advisor tends to narrate everything in the first person singular — "I fixed the pipeline," "I built the forecast" — because there was no team underneath them to share the win. The best fractional CROs are, in a sense, temporary — they measure success by what survives their departure, and it shows in how they speak about the people around them.

It's also worth stating out loud, on the first call, that you intend to run a paid trial before any longer commitment. Watch the reaction closely, because it's diagnostic in itself. A real operator hears "paid two-week diagnostic" and relaxes — it's a chance to prove value and scope honestly, and it's how they prefer to work anyway. A title-seller hears the same sentence and starts negotiating the trial away, bundling it into a longer retainer, or explaining why their process "doesn't really fit a short project." You will often learn more from that thirty-second exchange than from the previous twenty minutes of polished narrative.

## How do I tell a real fractional CRO from a repackaged consultant?
The fractional title has attracted a lot of adjacent professionals — sales trainers, agency owners, and slide-deck strategists — who use "fractional CRO" as a marketing label without ever having carried a number or owned a P&L. The distinction is not snobbery; it is survival, because a strategist who has never personally built a comp plan, sat in forecast calls, or fired an underperformer will give you advice that sounds right and fails in practice. The screen is simple: a real revenue operator has *owned outcomes*, not just advised on them.

The flowchart below is the practical filter. Run every candidate through it before you get to price. The key branch points are whether they have carried a quota or revenue target, whether they have built and managed a team rather than just coached one, and whether they will commit to a measurable 90-day outcome instead of billing purely for hours. Anyone who cannot clear all three is a consultant or trainer — which may still be valuable, but is not the same purchase.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Candidate says fractional CRO] --> B{Has carried a revenue target}
    B -->|No| C[Likely a strategist or trainer]
    B -->|Yes| D{Has built and managed a team}
    D -->|No| C
    D -->|Yes| E{Will commit to a 90 day outcome}
    E -->|No| F[Advisor not operator]
    E -->|Yes| G[Real fractional CRO worth trialing]
```

Two more tests separate operators from advisors. The first is **reference specificity** — ask for a former direct report and a former peer, not just a happy CEO, because the people who worked *under* and *beside* a revenue leader know whether the results were real. The second is **the trial project** — propose a paid two-to-four-week diagnostic before any long engagement. Real operators welcome it because it lets them prove value and scope the work honestly; people selling a title tend to resist scoping down because their value evaporates under close inspection. Our overview of [structuring a fractional trial](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11133) covers how to design that first project so it protects both sides.

A subtler version of the same problem is the operator who was genuinely excellent — five or ten years ago, at a company nothing like yours. Experience decays and it doesn't transfer cleanly across motions. A CRO who built a world-class outbound enterprise sales org in 2016 may have never run a modern product-led motion, and the playbooks that made them great can quietly misfire in a self-serve, usage-based world. This is why the "what motions have *you* run" question matters more than seniority or logos. Prestige on a résumé is not the same as relevance to your specific revenue problem, and the fractional market is full of impressive people whose impressive era doesn't match your present. Probe for *recent, adjacent* wins, not just famous ones.

Finally, be honest with yourself about the failure mode where the consultant is exactly right for you. If your real need is a diagnostic — you don't actually know why revenue is stuck and you want an expert to tell you — then a strategist or advisor may be the correct, cheaper purchase, and forcing that person into an "operator" frame just wastes money on execution capacity you won't use. The filter above isn't meant to shame advisors; it's meant to prevent a *mismatch*. Buy an operator when you need someone to build and run inside the company. Buy an advisor when you need a sharp outside diagnosis and can execute it yourself. The expensive mistakes happen when you buy one and needed the other.

## What will it cost, and who negotiates the terms?
Pricing in the fractional market is genuinely variable, so be wary of anyone quoting a precise universal number — rates depend on the operator's seniority, your stage, the hours committed, and whether you go through a firm or direct. In broad strokes, engagements are structured three ways: a **monthly retainer** for a set band of hours, a **day-rate** for lighter or project-based work, and increasingly a **retainer-plus-equity** blend for early-stage companies that want the operator invested in outcomes. The person you negotiate with depends on the channel — through a firm, you negotiate with the firm's engagement lead; direct, you negotiate with the operator. In both cases, get the scope, hours, term length, and an exit clause in writing.

The negotiation conversation should center on *outcomes and hours*, not just rate. A cheaper operator at five hours a week who can only advise is often more expensive per unit of progress than a pricier one at ten hours who actually builds. Ask how they handle the ramp-down: a good fractional CRO plans to make themselves progressively less necessary by hiring and training your full-time leader, so the engagement should have a natural taper built in. Watch for firms that structure contracts to maximize duration rather than resolve your problem — a taper clause and clear 90-day checkpoints keep incentives honest. If you are weighing fractional against a full-time hire on pure economics, model both against the specific revenue gap you are trying to close, not against each other in the abstract.

Pay attention to the *shape* of the equity conversation when it comes up, because it's a fast read on alignment. An operator who asks for a modest equity slice explicitly tied to hitting revenue milestones is telling you they expect to earn it and are willing to be measured. An operator who wants a large equity grant with no performance gates, front-loaded, is telling you something different. Neither is automatically wrong — early-stage cash constraints make equity-heavy deals reasonable — but the structure reveals whether the person is betting on the outcome or hedging against it. The healthiest arrangements usually blend a cash retainer that keeps the operator engaged week-to-week with a small, milestone-linked equity component that keeps their eyes on the twelve-month result.

Finally, budget for the *hidden* costs of a bad fit rather than optimizing purely for the sticker rate. The most expensive fractional engagement is the cheap one that runs for six months, produces slide decks instead of pipeline, and leaves your team no better trained than when it started. Against that risk, a paid two-to-four-week trial is not an added cost — it's insurance, and one of the highest-return few thousand dollars you'll spend in the whole process. Price the trial into your plan from the beginning, treat it as the real interview, and only sign a longer term once someone has actually delivered something measurable inside your company.

## What should the engagement look like once I pick someone?
Choosing the person is only half the job; structuring the engagement is what determines whether the hire pays off. The strongest fractional relationships open with a defined **diagnostic phase** — usually the first two to four weeks — where the operator does nothing but listen, pull data, sit in on calls, and interview the team before proposing a single change. Resist the urge to skip this. Founders who push a fractional CRO to "just start fixing things" on day one usually get motion without direction, because the operator is guessing at root causes instead of finding them. The diagnostic is where a real revenue leader earns their premium, and its output should be a short, written point of view: here is what's actually broken, here is the 90-day plan, here is how we'll measure it.

From there, insist on **rhythm and artifacts**. A well-run fractional engagement has a predictable cadence — a weekly working session, a standing forecast review, a monthly checkpoint against the 90-day goal — and it produces durable things the company keeps: a documented sales process, a comp plan, a hiring scorecard for the full-time leader who will eventually take over. Beware engagements that generate only meetings and advice with nothing left behind, because the entire point of a fractional CRO is to install operating systems your team runs after they leave. Set the taper expectation explicitly at the start: the ideal fractional CRO is working to make themselves unnecessary, and the clearest sign the money was well spent is that, six months later, someone on your team is running the machine they built and you no longer need the outside operator at all.

## Related questions
### How is a fractional CRO different from a sales consultant?
A fractional CRO owns revenue outcomes and operates inside your company as an interim executive, while a consultant advises from outside and hands you recommendations. The operator builds and runs; the consultant analyzes and departs.

### Should an early-stage startup hire a fractional CRO or a VP of Sales?
Pre-repeatable-motion, a fractional CRO who can *design* the go-to-market is usually better than a full-time VP hired to *execute* a motion that does not exist yet. Hire the VP once the model is proven.

### How many hours a week does a fractional CRO work?
Most engagements run roughly one to two days a week, often 8 to 16 hours, though intensive early diagnostics can run higher. More than four concurrent clients is a red flag for diluted attention.

### Can my board or investors introduce me to a fractional CRO?
Yes, and this is one of the highest-trust channels available. Investors pattern-match across their portfolio and often keep informal lists of operators they would back again, so a single warm intro can replace weeks of cold searching.

### What is the fastest way to hire a fractional CRO?
Call a specialized fractional-executive firm — they maintain a prescreened bench and can put a matched candidate in front of you within a week, trading a rate premium for speed and vetting.

## FAQ
**Who places fractional CROs?**
Specialized fractional-executive firms, fractional-talent marketplaces, your own founder network, your board and investors, and — as a last resort — generalist executive recruiters. The first four consistently outperform the fifth for revenue roles.

**Is a fractional CRO the same as an interim CRO?**
Not quite. Interim usually implies near-full-time coverage of a sudden gap, often to bridge until a permanent hire. Fractional is a deliberately part-time, ongoing arrangement designed around a set number of hours per week.

**How long does a typical fractional CRO engagement last?**
Commonly three to twelve months, structured to solve a specific problem and then taper as the operator hires and trains your eventual full-time leader. Beware open-ended contracts with no checkpoints.

**What should I prepare before the first call?**
A one-paragraph problem statement in revenue terms: what is breaking, what "fixed" looks like in 90 days, and roughly how many hours a week you think you need. This paragraph doubles as your screening tool.

**How do I check references for a fractional CRO?**
Ask for a former direct report and a former peer, not only a happy CEO. The people who worked under and beside the operator know whether the results were real and repeatable.

**Should I pay for a trial project first?**
Yes. A paid two-to-four-week diagnostic lets the operator prove value and scope the work honestly before you commit to a longer engagement. Real operators welcome it; title-sellers resist it.

**What questions separate an operator from an advisor?**
Ask whether they have personally carried a revenue target, built and managed a team, and will commit to a measurable 90-day outcome. Failing any of the three signals a strategist rather than a revenue operator.

**Can I hire a fractional CRO directly without a firm?**
Absolutely — direct hires through marketplaces or referrals lower cost and improve transparency, but they shift the vetting burden onto you. Budget extra time for reference checks and a trial project.

**How do I know when it's time to convert to a full-time CRO?**
When the go-to-market motion is repeatable, the team is running the systems the fractional operator installed, and the ceiling on growth is now capacity rather than design. At that point you want someone full-time to scale a proven machine.

**What's a fair way to structure equity for a fractional CRO?**
A small equity slice tied to specific revenue milestones, paired with a cash retainer, keeps incentives aligned. Be cautious of large front-loaded grants with no performance gates, which reward tenure rather than results.
